recentItems.title: M16A Schwarzlose: Austro-Hungarian WW1 Aircraft MG
recentItems.description:
One of the rare aircraft machine guns from the First World War is the Austro-Hungarian Schwarzlose. This was a delayed blowback heavy machine gun used by the Empire's infantry as the M1907/12, and it was really the only domestic machine gun available for use in aircraft at the time. While guns were initially used with slotted or intact water jackets, the blowback mechanism meant that the jacket could be easily removed without compromising functionality (unlike Maxim/Vickers designs that required muzzle support). Two iterations of naked-barrel aircraft Schwarzlose guns were made, the M16 and M16A, with iterative improvements in rate of fire and reliability at high altitudes. The M16A seen here was capable of up to 880 rpm and operation at 23,000 feet. Only a few hundred of these guns appear to have been produced, and they are very scarce today.

Many thanks tot he US National WW1 Museum & Memorial for pulling this example out of their exhibit for me to film! If you are in Kansas City, make sure to stop by and see the museum:
https://www.theworldwar.org

recentItems.title: America's Do-It-All Naval Gun: The 5 Inch Mk12 on the USS New Jersey
recentItems.description:
The Mk12 5 inch, 38 caliber gun was one of the triumphs of American naval weaponry from World War Two. First used in 1934, it remained a standard weapon on new vessels until 1948. It used a 55 lb shell with a separate case that was manually loaded but power-rammed, allowing a high rate of fire from -15 to +85 degree angles of elevation. Coupled with the sophisticated fire control computers in US warships, it was one of the most effective anti-aircraft weapons in US inventory even before the introduction of radar proximity-fused shells in 1943. More than 8,000 of these guns were built by the end of World War Two, fitted to everything from merchant mariners to battleships like the USS New Jersey.

Make sure to check out the USS New Jersey Museum's channel for tons more information on the ship!
https://www.youtube.com/battleshipnewjersey

recentItems.title: Intro to EOTech: How Holographic Sights Actually Work
recentItems.description:
Holograms are pretty close to space magic, but today I will try to explain how they work in an understandable way. They have also proven surprisingly difficult to find commercial use for, but  one program at the University of Michigan Ann Arbor led to the creation of EOTech to produce holographic weapon sights. So once we (hopefully) have a better understanding of how these sights work, we will look at how they differ from red dot sights, and why their specific pros and cons are.

recentItems.title: Saudi Gold Plated Presentation G3: Gaudy or Elegant?
recentItems.description:
The Saudi Arabian government signed a contract with H&K to license domestic production of the G3 rifle at the Al Kharj factory complex in 1972. Production included standard rifles for general use, but also chrome- and gold-plated examples used as presentation pieces and diplomatic gifts. This is one of the gold examples, with deep decorative carving in the wood and gold plating on a number of parts, including the bolt carrier, charging handle, takedown pins, sling plate, and others. This one was made in 1988, and is serial number 00237. 

Saudi G3 production never did reach fully independent status, and used many semi-finished parts imported from Germany. Production of the MP5 and G36 were added later (1987 and 2008 respectively), but a diplomatic scandal in 2013 led Germany to cut off parts support.

Many thanks to the IRCGN (Institut de Recherche Criminelle de la Gendarmerie Nationale) for allowing me access to film this very rare rifle for you!

recentItems.title: Moroccan Unique Rr51 at the Hot Summer BUG Match
recentItems.description:
It's pretty hot out here in the southern Arizona summer, so I figured I'd lean into it. For the BUG Match this month, I have an-Moroccan police Unique Rr51. This is a simple blowback .32 ACP pistol made by MAPH in a bunch of variations for many decades. It holds 9 rounds in the magazine, and I've paired it with a vaguely North African Foreign Legion set of kit just for fun.

Ultimately, the match went amazingly well until that last stage. My 9 rounds was not enough to complete the course of fire there, and it was worth so many points that it outweighed all the other stages. Ah well...
